result.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers explain why boxes add noise and offer the same core alternatives with concrete pixel values. B is clearer about when a card is justified: it names real objects users open, select, drag or compare, and it adds the 'one of border, shadow or fill' rule. Its ordered 'stop at the first that works' list and practical tips (CSS gap, the squint test) make it slightly more useful. A lists more alternatives, but several overlap, and it treats shadows as an alternative even though it admits a shadow still makes a container. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers explain the noise and competition problem well, and both give concrete pixel values. A does better on when a card is justified: it gives clear criteria (users open, select, drag or compare the item, or it must stand out from a busy background) and orders the alternatives so the reader knows when to stop. B lists more alternatives but adds less useful ones like shadows and accent edges, and its card guidance is a bit thinner, though it does name examples such as grid items and modals.
